integration_questions: Is the sensor span (6 cm) wide enough, or does the signal saturate or drop out on the sharpest bends?
Does a 5 cm forward sensor lead cause any delay or phase lag that makes steering oscillate at higher base speeds?
Which sensor weight pattern was easiest to tune, and was a 12 mm footprint sufficient?
Did the 0.8 kg mass and 12 cm wheel track give enough turn authority, or did the robot understeer or saturate the wheels?
feedback_request.requested_format: Brief notes on each question, plus the sensor and wheel changes you would make if you could change only one thing.

intent: Establish a symmetric, bounded baseline: five forward-mounted sensors spanning 6 cm, 12 mm footprints, mid-range wheel track, wheel radius, body and mass. The goal is to measure how the Integrator's controller behaves on this platform, and to see whether sensing span, sensor lead distance or drivetrain size is the limit on completion time and tracking error. I expect a completed run on the oval and s-bend tracks, with the slalom as the most likely source of line loss.
learning: No race data yet. Baseline hypotheses to test: (1) a wider sensor span reduces line loss on slalom bends; (2) a longer forward lead (larger y) improves stability at high speed but may reduce sharpness of response; (3) a lower mass or smaller wheel track increases turn rate and may reduce completion time. Measurements to request next: line_loss_events, rms_error, max_error, completion_time and steering_oscillation on each development track.
rationale: This is the first iteration, so there is no race telemetry or integration feedback yet. I am choosing a conventional, bounded baseline that the Integrator can build on and that gives clear evidence to read back. Five sensors spread at x = -0.03, -0.015, 0, 0.015 and 0.03 m give a 0.06 m sensing span, about 2.4 times the 25 mm tape width, so the line stays visible through moderate lateral error and the signal stays roughly linear near centre. The sensors sit at y = 0.05 m, ahead of the axle, so the line is read before the wheels reach it, which gives the controller lead time. Sensor size 0.012 m is about half the tape width: small enough for a crisp signal, large enough to avoid losing the line between sensors. Wheel track 0.12 m and wheel radius 0.03 m are mid-range, giving moderate turn authority and a moderate top speed. Mass 0.8 kg is a middle value that keeps yaw inertia modest. Body width 0.12 m and body length 0.16 m are mid-range. Body width has no effect on the off-track limit here, because max(0.06, 0.0125 + width/4) equals 0.06 for every width under 0.19 m. Expected result: a completed run on the development tracks, with rms_error well under 0.05 m and few line-loss events. The main risk is high-speed oscillation on the tighter slalom bends. I have not chosen a controller, as my role requires.
